claim: The subiculum pyramidal cell population can be deconstructed into eight separable subclasses using single-cell RNA-seq.
source: Using single-cell RNA-seq, we find that the subiculum pyramidal cell population can be deconstructed into eight separable subclasses.
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing nine clusters, with eight corresponding to subiculum pyramidal cells (one cluster was identified as CA1 cells).

claim: The transcriptomically defined subclasses are mapped onto abutting spatial domains.
source: These subclasses were mapped onto abutting spatial domains, ultimately producing a complex laminar and columnar organization with heterogeneity across classical dorsal-ventral, proximal-distal, and superficial-deep axes.
evidence: Two-color ISH experiments demonstrated that subclasses occupy mutually exclusive, abutting spatial domains (Figure 5).

claim: The transcriptomically defined subclasses correspond to differential protein products.
source: We further show that these transcriptomically defined subclasses correspond to differential protein products and can be associated with specific projection targets.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry experiments showed that transcript-level differences corresponded to differential protein products (Figure 8).

claim: The transcriptomically defined subclasses can be associated with specific projection targets.
source: We further show that these transcriptomically defined subclasses correspond to differential protein products and can be associated with specific projection targets.
evidence: Projection mapping experiments showed differential distribution of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters (Figure 9).

claim: The hippocampus has been studied extensively for its critical roles in episodic memory.
source: This brain region has been studied extensively for its critical roles in episodic memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957), spatial navigation (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), and emotionally motivated behavior (Kjelstrup et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scoville and Milner, 1957.

claim: The hippocampus has been studied extensively for its critical roles in spatial navigation.
source: This brain region has been studied extensively for its critical roles in episodic memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957), spatial navigation (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), and emotionally motivated behavior (Kjelstrup et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978.

claim: The hippocampus has been studied extensively for its critical roles in emotionally motivated behavior.
source: This brain region has been studied extensively for its critical roles in episodic memory (Scoville and Milner, 1957), spatial navigation (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), and emotionally motivated behavior (Kjelstrup et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kjelstrup et al., 2002.

claim: Evidence is emerging that suggests heterogeneity within classical cell types of the hippocampus may be an important feature for mediating hippocampal computation and function.
source: To date, evidence is emerging that suggests heterogeneity within classical cell types of the hippocampus may be an important feature for mediating hippocampal computation and function (Cembrowski et al., 2016a; Cembrowski et al., 2016b; Danielson et al., 2016; Igarashi et al., 2014; Knierim et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018; Strange et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The pyramidal cell type of the subiculum acts as an output from the hippocampus to a wide array of downstream targets.
source: One of these classical cell types is the pyramidal cell type of the subiculum, which acts as an output from the hippocampus to a wide array of downstream targets (Aggleton and Christiansen, 2015; Naber and Witter, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aggleton and Christiansen, 2015 and Naber and Witter, 1998.

claim: The dorsal pole of the subiculum can be partitioned into distinct proximal and distal subregions.
source: We recently found that the dorsal pole of the subiculum can be partitioned into distinct proximal and distal subregions (Cembrowski et al., 2018), motivating us to investigate whether additional heterogeneity could be revealed when considering the full spatial extent of the subiculum.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cembrowski et al., 2018.

claim: The proximal subiculum is composed of a molecular layer and multiple cell body layers, each distinguished by molecular and morphological differences.
source: Indeed, recent investigations using immunohistochemical labeling argue that the proximal subiculum is composed of a molecular layer and multiple cell body layers, each distinguished by molecular and morphological differences, while the distal subiculum is more uniform (Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016.

claim: The distal subiculum is more uniform than the proximal subiculum.
source: Indeed, recent investigations using immunohistochemical labeling argue that the proximal subiculum is composed of a molecular layer and multiple cell body layers, each distinguished by molecular and morphological differences, while the distal subiculum is more uniform (Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016.

claim: Specific downstream projections change across space in the subiculum.
source: Additionally, as specific downstream projections and postulated functional contributions change across space in the subiculum (Böhm et al., 2018; Bubb et al., 2017; Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016; Naber and Witter, 1998; O'Mara et al., 2009), understanding subicular organizational rules will likely be critical for a cell-type-specific deconstruction of memory, cognition, and emotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Postulated functional contributions change across space in the subiculum.
source: Additionally, as specific downstream projections and postulated functional contributions change across space in the subiculum (Böhm et al., 2018; Bubb et al., 2017; Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016; Naber and Witter, 1998; O'Mara et al., 2009), understanding subicular organizational rules will likely be critical for a cell-type-specific deconstruction of memory, cognition, and emotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: High-read-depth, high-quality transcriptomes were obtained from 1150 cells with 5.6 ± 1.0 thousand expressed genes per cell.
source: This approach obtained high-read-depth, high-quality transcriptomes from 1150 cells (5.6 ± 1.0 thousand expressed genes/cell, mean ± SD).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of cells and genes per cell obtained from scRNA-seq experiments.

claim: Nine clusters were identified that expressed marker genes associated with excitatory neurons.
source: From this analysis, nine clusters were identified that expressed marker genes associated with excitatory neurons (e.g. Camk2a, Slc17a7; Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; note 14 putative non-neuronal cells and 13 putative interneurons were excluded from analysis, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of nine clusters from graph-based clustering analysis.

claim: Single genes were largely sufficient to delineate individual clusters.
source: Remarkably, single genes were largely sufficient to delineate individual clusters (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript shows that individual marker genes can distinguish clusters in Figure 2B.

claim: Relatively large subclasses of cells were delineated by the marker genes S100b, Dlk1, Tpbg, and Fn1.
source: Relatively large subclasses of cells were delineated by the marker genes S100b, Dlk1, Tpbg, and Fn1.
evidence: The manuscript identifies these marker genes as delineating large subclasses based on scRNA-seq data.

claim: Smaller subclasses showed expression of Gpc3, Cbln4, Lefty1, Spink8, and Ly6g6e.
source: Smaller subclasses, putatively corresponding to rarer subclasses of excitatory cells, showed expression of Gpc3, Cbln4, Lefty1, Spink8, and Ly6g6e.
evidence: The manuscript identifies these marker genes as delineating smaller subclasses based on scRNA-seq data.

claim: A given cluster exhibited enrichment of 50 ± 32 genes on average relative to the remaining dataset.
source: On average, a given cluster exhibited enrichment of 50 ± 32 genes relative to the remaining dataset (defined as >3 fold enriched on average and pADJ <0.05; see Materials and methods), and 114 ± 68 genes when restricting analysis to pairwise cluster comparisons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of differentially expressed genes across clusters.

claim: A given cluster exhibited enrichment of 114 ± 68 genes on average when restricting analysis to pairwise cluster comparisons.
source: On average, a given cluster exhibited enrichment of 50 ± 32 genes relative to the remaining dataset (defined as >3 fold enriched on average and pADJ <0.05; see Materials and methods), and 114 ± 68 genes when restricting analysis to pairwise cluster comparisons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of differentially expressed genes across clusters.

claim: Data from 847 excitatory neurons were gathered from five additional animals for replicate cross-validation.
source: From these animals, we dissected the subiculum and gathered data from a total of 847 excitatory neurons (5.6 ± 0.8 thousand genes expressed/cell; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of cells obtained from replicate experiments.

claim: Eight clusters were obtained from the replicate dataset.
source: We performed analysis of this dataset identically to our previous dataset, and obtained eight clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of clusters identified in the replicate dataset.

claim: All eight clusters from the replicate dataset had marker genes associated with clusters obtained from the original dataset.
source: All eight clusters had marker genes associated with clusters obtained from our original dataset (geometric mean pADJ values for cluster-specific markers = 8.7e-40, cf. pADJ = 4.1e-62 from original dataset; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of marker genes between original and replicate datasets.

claim: The single cluster from original dataset that was missed in the replicate dataset was associated with Cbln4 expression.
source: The single cluster from original dataset that was missed in the replicate dataset, associated with Cbln4 expression, was detected in a subset of cells that separated in t-SNE space but failed to cluster at our predetermined resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the Cbln4 cluster in the replicate dataset.

claim: No new clusters emerged from the replicate dataset.
source: Importantly, no new clusters emerged from this replicate dataset, illustrating that our original scRNA-seq dataset accurately predicted subpopulation-specific organization in entirely separate animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of clusters between original and replicate datasets.

claim: The marker genes Gpc3, Dlk1, and Tpbg were strongly expressed ventrally in anterior sections.
source: The marker genes Gpc3, Dlk1, and Tpbg were strongly expressed ventrally in anterior sections, with Dlk1 and Tpbg exhibiting dorsal expression in more posterior sections.
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images from the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas.

claim: Dlk1 and Tpbg exhibited dorsal expression in more posterior sections.
source: The marker genes Gpc3, Dlk1, and Tpbg were strongly expressed ventrally in anterior sections, with Dlk1 and Tpbg exhibiting dorsal expression in more posterior sections.
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images from the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas.

claim: Col5a2 and S100b were expressed in disparate populations of dorsal proximal subiculum.
source: Alternatively, Col5a2 and S100b were expressed in disparate populations of dorsal proximal subiculum (i.e., close to CA1), whereas Fn1 was enriched in distal subiculum (i.e. away from CA1) (Cembrowski et al., 2018) (note that in coronal sections, distal subiculum is primarily associated with enrichment in posterior sections; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images.

claim: Fn1 was enriched in distal subiculum.
source: Alternatively, Col5a2 and S100b were expressed in disparate populations of dorsal proximal subiculum (i.e., close to CA1), whereas Fn1 was enriched in distal subiculum (i.e. away from CA1) (Cembrowski et al., 2018) (note that in coronal sections, distal subiculum is primarily associated with enrichment in posterior sections; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images and cites previous work.

claim: Ly6g6e labeled the deepest layer of cells across the long axis.
source: The gene Ly6g6e labeled the deepest layer of cells across the long axis, and Cbln4 corresponding to a layer of cells in the posterior subiculum.
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images.

claim: Cbln4 corresponded to a layer of cells in the posterior subiculum.
source: The gene Ly6g6e labeled the deepest layer of cells across the long axis, and Cbln4 corresponding to a layer of cells in the posterior subiculum.
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images.

claim: Each marker gene corresponded to a continuous spatial subregion of the subiculum.
source: Thus, each of these marker genes corresponded to a continuous spatial subregion of the subiculum (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cluster of cells associated with Myo5b expression likely belonged to CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Thus, the cluster of cells associated with Myo5b expression likely belonged to CA1 pyramidal cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides ISH and RNA-seq evidence showing Myo5b expression in CA1 cells.

claim: No other clusters exhibited markers associated with off-target gene expression.
source: Importantly, no other clusters exhibited markers associated with off-target gene expression (e.g. inhibitory neurons, Figure 2B; pre-, para-, or postsubiculum, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of marker gene expression to exclude off-target cell types.

claim: ZnT3, Nos, and Pcp4 all conformed to specific proximal laminae.
source: Specifically, it was shown that ZnT3, Nos, and Pcp4 (encoded by Slc30a3, Nos1, and Pcp4, respectively) all conformed to specific proximal laminae, whereas Vglut2 (encoding by Slc17a6) corresponded to the distal subiculum.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous IHC work by Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016 and validates it with scRNA-seq data.

claim: Vglut2 corresponded to the distal subiculum.
source: Specifically, it was shown that ZnT3, Nos, and Pcp4 (encoded by Slc30a3, Nos1, and Pcp4, respectively) all conformed to specific proximal laminae, whereas Vglut2 (encoding by Slc17a6) corresponded to the distal subiculum.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous IHC work by Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016 and validates it with scRNA-seq data.

claim: Expression of Slc30a3, Nos1, Pcp4, and Slc17a6 corresponded to specific subclasses and obeyed the spatial organization expected by IHC.
source: We verified that expression of these genes corresponded to specific subclasses and obeyed the spatial organization expected by IHC (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of previous IHC findings using scRNA-seq and ISH data.

claim: Col5a2, Tpbg, and Ly6g6e seemingly corresponded to three distinct laminae in the dorsal subiculum, patterning the subiculum in a superficial-to-deep fashion.
source: Inspecting the dorsal subiculum first, we found that Col5a2, Tpbg, and Ly6g6e seemingly corresponded to three distinct laminae, patterning the subiculum in a superficial-to-deep fashion (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the ventral subiculum, the combination of Cbln4, Dlk1, Tpbg, and Ly6g6e defined a laminar subiculum organization.
source: Similarly, in the ventral subiculum the combination of Cbln4, Dlk1, Tpbg, and Ly6g6e defined a laminar subiculum organization (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial expression patterns based on ISH images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 99% of 772 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion between Tpbg and Gpc3 expression.
source: Using this strategy, we verified that these laminae corresponded to distinct, abutting but non-overlapping populations of cells (99% of 772 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, n = 2 mice, two sections/mouse; Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of two-color ISH experiments.

claim: 98% of 457 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion between Fn1 and Dlk1 expression.
source: Similar reciprocal laminar organization could be identified for additional marker genes and associated subclasses (Fn1 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 457 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5B; Tpbg vs. Dlk1: 97% of 801 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5C; Cbln4 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 489 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5D; Tpbg vs. Ly6g6e: 93% of 733 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5E; all statistics represent results from n = 2 mice, two sections/mouse).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of two-color ISH experiments.

claim: 97% of 801 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion between Tpbg and Dlk1 expression.
source: Similar reciprocal laminar organization could be identified for additional marker genes and associated subclasses (Fn1 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 457 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5B; Tpbg vs. Dlk1: 97% of 801 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5C; Cbln4 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 489 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5D; Tpbg vs. Ly6g6e: 93% of 733 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5E; all statistics represent results from n = 2 mice, two sections/mouse).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of two-color ISH experiments.

claim: 98% of 489 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion between Cbln4 and Dlk1 expression.
source: Similar reciprocal laminar organization could be identified for additional marker genes and associated subclasses (Fn1 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 457 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5B; Tpbg vs. Dlk1: 97% of 801 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5C; Cbln4 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 489 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5D; Tpbg vs. Ly6g6e: 93% of 733 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5E; all statistics represent results from n = 2 mice, two sections/mouse).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of two-color ISH experiments.

claim: 93% of 733 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion between Tpbg and Ly6g6e expression.
source: Similar reciprocal laminar organization could be identified for additional marker genes and associated subclasses (Fn1 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 457 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5B; Tpbg vs. Dlk1: 97% of 801 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5C; Cbln4 vs. Dlk1: 98% of 489 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5D; Tpbg vs. Ly6g6e: 93% of 733 labeled cells exhibited mutual exclusion, Figure 5E; all statistics represent results from n = 2 mice, two sections/mouse).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of two-color ISH experiments.

claim: Most clusters (6/8) exhibited marker gene expression that traversed most or all of the hippocampal long axis.
source: This analysis revealed that most clusters (6/8) exhibited marker gene expression that traversed most or all of the hippocampal long axis (Figure 6, top).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of marker gene expression across the dorsal-ventral axis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Transcriptomic clusters associated with S100b and Gpc3 respectively spanned the dorsal and ventral halves of the subiculum.
source: The only exceptions to this rule were transcriptomic clusters associated with S100b and Gpc3, which respectively spanned the dorsal and ventral halves of the subiculum (Figure 6, bottom).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of marker gene expression across the dorsal-ventral axis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The primary axes of variation in the subiculum were superficial-deep and proximal-distal.
source: Thus, in total, the transcriptomically identified subclasses of subPCs produced a complex geometry that exhibited heterogeneity in the dorsal-ventral, superficial-deep, and proximal-distal axes (Figure 7; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1). However, given that most subclasses traversed the dorsal-ventral axis, the primary axes of variation were superficial-deep and proximal-distal (Witter, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that most subclasses traverse the dorsal-ventral axis.

claim: Kv4.3 was depleted in distal subiculum.
source: We found that Kv4.3, a potassium channel pore-forming subunit encoded by Kcnd3, was depleted in distal subiculum (i.e. the Fn1-associated cluster 4) (Figure 8A, left).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC results showing Kv4.3 protein distribution.

claim: Distal subiculum was enriched for synaptotagmin-2.
source: Conversely, this region was enriched for synaptotagmin-2 (a calcium sensor that mediates vesicular release, encoding by Syt2) and Vglut2 (a glutamate transporter encoded by Slc17a6) (Figure 8A, middle and right) (Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC results showing synaptotagmin-2 protein distribution.

claim: Distal subiculum was enriched for Vglut2.
source: Conversely, this region was enriched for synaptotagmin-2 (a calcium sensor that mediates vesicular release, encoding by Syt2) and Vglut2 (a glutamate transporter encoded by Slc17a6) (Figure 8A, middle and right) (Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC results showing Vglut2 protein distribution.

claim: Slc17a6 expression can be exploited for subclass-specific access of the distal subiculum in transgenic mice.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the Slc17a6 expression could be exploited for subclass-specific access of the distal subiculum in transgenic mice (Vong et al., 2011), providing direct evidence that our transcriptomic work can be leveraged to target and manipulate specific cell types (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) (see also Cembrowski et al., 2018; Yamawaki et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript reports experiments using Slc17a6-IRES-cre mice to target distal subiculum cells.

claim: The calcium peptide S100 was found in dendrites and cell bodies of the cluster associated with marker gene S100b.
source: Interestingly, the calcium peptide S100, typically used as an astrocyte marker, was found in dendrites and cell bodies of the cluster associated with marker gene S100b (Figure 8B; see Figure 8—figure supplement 2 for expansion).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC results showing S100 protein distribution.

claim: Glypican 3 was located ventrally and corresponded to a specific lamina.
source: Glypican 3, encoded by Gpc3, was located ventrally and corresponded to a specific lamina (Figure 8C).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC results showing Glypican 3 protein distribution.

claim: Purkinje Cell Protein 4 and Pamr1 exhibited deep lamina-specific enrichment.
source: The proteins Purkinje Cell Protein 4 (Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016) and Pamr1, both associated with markers of deep subiculum neurons, exhibited deep lamina-specific enrichment.
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC results showing Pcp4 and Pamr1 protein distribution.

claim: Cells from PFC, NA, and amygdala projections were differentially distributed across transcriptomic clusters.
source: Cells from these projections were differentially distributed across transcriptomic clusters (Figure 9; see also Figure 9—figure supplement 1 for replicate cross-validation).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters shown in Figure 9.

claim: Both PFC and NA projections tended to be relatively diffusely spread across clusters.
source: Broadly, both PFC and NA projections tended to be relatively diffusely spread across clusters, although each projection was notably absent from specific subpopulations (e.g. NA projections were Tpbg-negative; see Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters.

claim: NA projections were Tpbg-negative.
source: Broadly, both PFC and NA projections tended to be relatively diffusely spread across clusters, although each projection was notably absent from specific subpopulations (e.g. NA projections were Tpbg-negative; see Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis showing NA projections lack Tpbg expression.

claim: 86% of amygdala-projecting cells were within the Gpc3 cluster.
source: In contrast, amygdala-projecting cells were largely associated with a single dedicated transcriptomic subclass (86% of amygdala-projecting cells were within the Gpc3 cluster, relative to 8% and 17% of NA- and PFC-projecting cells).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters.

claim: 8% of NA-projecting cells were within the Gpc3 cluster.
source: In contrast, amygdala-projecting cells were largely associated with a single dedicated transcriptomic subclass (86% of amygdala-projecting cells were within the Gpc3 cluster, relative to 8% and 17% of NA- and PFC-projecting cells).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters.

claim: 17% of PFC-projecting cells were within the Gpc3 cluster.
source: In contrast, amygdala-projecting cells were largely associated with a single dedicated transcriptomic subclass (86% of amygdala-projecting cells were within the Gpc3 cluster, relative to 8% and 17% of NA- and PFC-projecting cells).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters.

claim: Ly6g6e and Col5a2 clusters were completely devoid of projections for all surveyed downstream regions.
source: Some transcriptomic subpopulations were completely devoid of projections for all surveyed downstream regions (e.g. Ly6g6e and Col5a2 clusters; see Figure 9—figure supplement 3 for overview), suggesting that they may correspond to other extrahippocampal projections (Cembrowski et al., 2018) and/or function as local excitatory neurons (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of projection-labeled cells across transcriptomic clusters.

claim: 97% of labeled cells were mutually exclusive for Tpbg expression and NA projections.
source: Overall, 97% of labeled cells were mutually exclusive for Tpbg expression and PFC projections (n = 275 total cells from n = 2 animals).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of two-color ISH combined with retrograde labeling shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: The subiculum can be deconstructed into proximal and distal subdomains, with further laminar organization predominantly found in proximal subiculum.
source: Thus, the subiculum can be deconstructed into proximal and distal subdomains, with further laminar organization predominantly found in proximal subiculum (as previously proposed by Ishihara and Fukuda, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes findings from scRNA-seq and ISH to describe the organizational structure of the subiculum.

claim: At least six discretely separable subclasses of subiculum pyramidal cells exist.
source: Here, we directly demonstrated the discrete pairwise separation of five clusters (Figure 5), and the overall nonoverlapping nature of these clusters can be inferred from their relative spatial ordering. Taking these results in combination with previous in situ hybridization (Cembrowski et al., 2018), this demonstrates the existence of at least six discretely separable subclasses of subiculum pyramidal cells.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from two-color ISH experiments and previous work.

claim: The eight scRNA-seq subclasses resolved likely represent an approximation (and potentially, a lower bound) as to the ultimate number of true biological subclasses of subiculum pyramidal cells.
source: As a result, the eight scRNA-seq subclasses resolved here likely represent an approximation (and potentially, a lower bound) as to the ultimate number of true biological subclasses of subiculum pyramidal cells.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the completeness of subclass identification based on methodological considerations.

claim: Heterogeneity within each classical hippocampal cell type encompasses both discrete and continuous variation across dorsal-ventral, proximal-distal, and superficial-deep axes.
source: This heterogeneity encompasses both discrete and continuous variation across dorsal-ventral, proximal-distal, and superficial-deep axes (Cembrowski et al., 2016a; Cembrowski et al., 2018; Cembrowski et al., 2016b; Habib et al., 2016; Thompson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous transcriptomic research.

claim: Transcriptomic identity can be coherently aligned with specialized functionality.
source: As higher order cellular, circuit, and functional features also vary in related ways (Cembrowski and Spruston, 2018b, in review; Danielson et al., 2016; Knierim et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018; Strange et al., 2014), this suggests that transcriptomic identity can be coherently aligned with specialized functionality (Cembrowski et al., 2018; Yamawaki et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from citations to previous work showing covariation of transcriptomic and functional features.

claim: The transcriptomically defined subclasses identified in this study likely vary according to higher-order structure and function.
source: It follows that the transcriptomically defined subclasses identified in this study likely vary according to higher-order structure and function.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from widespread differential expression of functionally relevant genes and covariation with protein products and projections.

claim: In the proximal subiculum, transcriptomically discrete subclasses of cells occupy abutting laminae.
source: In the proximal subiculum (e.g. proximal to Fn1-expressing cells, which define the most distal subclass; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), transcriptomically discrete subclasses of cells occupy abutting laminae (Figures 5 and 7).
evidence: The manuscript reports this based on two-color ISH experiments and spatial mapping.

claim: In the distal subiculum, gene expression tends to be relatively homogeneous.
source: In the distal subiculum, gene expression tends to be relatively homogeneous (although note a lamina of Tpbg-expressing cells in posterior subiculum: Figures 3 and 7).
evidence: The manuscript reports this based on ISH and scRNA-seq data.

claim: The scRNA-seq data are publicly hosted in conjunction with analysis and visualization tools at http://hipposeq.janelia.org.
source: Data from these cells, in conjunction with user-friendly analysis and visualization tools, are available on http://hipposeq.janelia.org.
evidence: The manuscript states that data and tools are publicly available at the specified URL.

claim: Raw and processed scRNA-seq datasets have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus under GEO: GSE113069.
source: Raw and processed scRNA-seq datasets have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus under GEO: GSE113069.
evidence: The manuscript states that data have been deposited in a public repository.

claim: All analysis scripts are publicly available at DOI:10.6084/m9.figshare.7140350.
source: All analysis scripts are publicly available (DOI:10.6084/m9.figshare.7140350) (Cembrowski and Spruston, 2018c).
evidence: The manuscript states that analysis scripts are publicly available at the specified DOI.
